# Generalized Sum with Countable Non-zero Summands / Corollary

## 0. The statement, and how it must be read

**Claim as given.** Let $V$ be a Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|$, let $(v_i)_{i\in I}$ be an indexed
family in $V$, and let $J,K\subseteq I$ be countably infinite with
$S:=\{i\in I: v_i\neq 0\}\subseteq J\cap K$. Let $\{j_0,j_1,j_2,\dots\}$ and $\{k_0,k_1,k_2,\dots\}$ be
countably infinite enumerations of $J$ and $K$, and let $r\in\mathbb R_{>0}$. Then
$\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_{j_n}$ converges absolutely to $r$ iff $\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_{k_n}$ converges
absolutely to $r$.

Three points of reading must be settled before anything can be proved.

**(i) Enumerations.** Following the ProofWiki convention $\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$, a *countably
infinite enumeration* of a countably infinite set $J$ is a bijection $\mathbb N\to J$, $n\mapsto j_n$.
In particular the terms $j_0,j_1,j_2,\dots$ are pairwise distinct and exhaust $J$; likewise for $K$.
The enumerations are indexed from $0$, as the notation $j_0,k_0$ shows.

**(ii) The index range of the series.** The series in the claim are written $\sum_{n=1}^\infty$, i.e.
they *omit* the terms $v_{j_0}$ and $v_{k_0}$. Read literally, the claim is **false**; see §1. The
off-by-one is a transcription slip: the intended series run over the whole enumeration,
$\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{j_n}$ and $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{k_n}$. With that correction the claim is true,
and §2–§4 prove it in a sharp form.

**(iii) "converges absolutely to $r$".** A series $\sum_n a_n$ in a normed space *converges
absolutely* iff $\sum_n\|a_n\|$ converges in $\mathbb R$. The phrase "converges absolutely to $r$"
with $r\in\mathbb R_{>0}$ is type-ambiguous: it can mean

* (A) the series converges absolutely and its sum (an element of $V$) is $r$ — which presupposes
  $r\in V$; or
* (B) the series converges absolutely and the sum of the norms is $r$, i.e. $\sum_n\|a_n\|=r$ — this
  is the reading under which "$r\in\mathbb R_{>0}$" is literally meaningful for an arbitrary $V$.

We do not have to choose. The Main Theorem below proves that the two series have *the same vector
sum and the same sum of norms*; consequently the biconditional holds under (A), under (B), and under
any other reading that is a property of the pair (vector sum, sum of norms). The hypothesis $r>0$ is
never needed.

Throughout, for a finite set $F$ of indices we write $\sum_{i\in F}v_i$ and $\sum_{i\in F}\|v_i\|$ for
the (unambiguous, since $V$ is an abelian group and $\mathbb R$ is) finite sums, with the empty sum
equal to $0$.

## 1. The literal reading (series from $n=1$) is false

Take $V=\mathbb R$ with $\|x\|=|x|$, which is a Banach space, and $I=\mathbb N$. Put
$$v_5=1,\qquad v_i=0\ \ (i\neq5),$$
so that $S=\{i:v_i\neq0\}=\{5\}$. Take
$$J=\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\dots\},\qquad K=\{5,6,7,\dots\},$$
both countably infinite subsets of $I$ with $S=\{5\}\subseteq J\cap K=K$. Enumerate each in increasing
order — the canonical choice, so no artificial reordering is involved:
$$j_n=n\ \ (n\in\mathbb N),\qquad k_n=n+5\ \ (n\in\mathbb N);$$
these are bijections $\mathbb N\to J$ and $\mathbb N\to K$. Let $r=1\in\mathbb R_{>0}$.

The terms of the first series are $v_{j_n}=v_n$ for $n\ge1$, and exactly one of them, namely $v_5=1$,
is non-zero; hence
$$\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_{j_n}=1=r,\qquad \sum_{n=1}^\infty\|v_{j_n}\|=1=r,$$
so $\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_{j_n}$ converges absolutely to $r$ under reading (A) (legitimate here, since
$V=\mathbb R$) and under reading (B). The terms of the second series are $v_{k_n}=v_{n+5}$ for
$n\ge1$, i.e. $v_6,v_7,v_8,\dots$, all of which vanish, because the only non-zero member $v_5=v_{k_0}$
of the family is carried by the *omitted* index $n=0$; hence
$$\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_{k_n}=0\neq r,\qquad \sum_{n=1}^\infty\|v_{k_n}\|=0\neq r .$$
So the right-hand side of the claimed biconditional fails while the left-hand side holds, under either
reading of "converges absolutely to $r$". The claim as literally written is therefore false.

**Remark 1.1.** The phenomenon is not an artefact of taking $J\ne K$. With $I=\mathbb N$, $v_0=1$ and
$v_i=0$ for $i\ge1$, and $J=K=\mathbb N$ enumerated by $j_n=n$ and by $k_0=1,\ k_1=0,\ k_n=n\ (n\ge2)$
— two enumerations of the *same* set — one gets $\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_{j_n}=0$ while
$\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_{k_n}=1$, and likewise for the series of norms.

The failure is caused solely by the omission of the $0$-th terms; what survives of the literal
statement is recorded in Corollary 4.3.

## 2. The Main Theorem

> **Main Theorem.** Let $V$ be a Banach space with norm $\|\cdot\|$, let $(v_i)_{i\in I}$ be an
> indexed family of elements of $V$, and put $S:=\{i\in I: v_i\neq0\}$. Let $J,K\subseteq I$ be
> countably infinite sets with $S\subseteq J\cap K$, and let $n\mapsto j_n$ and $n\mapsto k_n$ be
> enumerations (bijections from $\mathbb N$) of $J$ and of $K$ respectively. Put
> $$M:=\sup\Big\{\textstyle\sum_{i\in F}\|v_i\| \;:\; F\subseteq S\ \text{finite}\Big\}\in[0,+\infty].$$
> Then:
> 1. $\sum_{n=0}^\infty\|v_{j_n}\|$ converges if and only if $M<\infty$, and in that case
>    $\sum_{n=0}^\infty\|v_{j_n}\|=M$. The same holds for $K$. In particular
>    $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{j_n}$ converges absolutely iff $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{k_n}$ does, and then
>    the two sums of norms are equal (both $=M$).
> 2. If $M<\infty$ then both series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{j_n}$ and $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{k_n}$
>    converge in $V$ and have the same sum.

Note that $M$ depends only on the family $(v_i)_{i\in I}$ — not on $J$, $K$, or the enumerations —
which is the whole point.

### Lemma 2.1 (absolute convergence implies convergence in a Banach space)

*Let $(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a sequence in a Banach space $V$ with $\sum_{n=0}^\infty\|a_n\|<\infty$.
Then $\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n$ converges in $V$.*

*Proof.* Let $s_N=\sum_{n=0}^N a_n$ and $t_N=\sum_{n=0}^N\|a_n\|$. By hypothesis $(t_N)$ converges,
hence is Cauchy. For $N>N'$, the triangle inequality gives
$$\|s_N-s_{N'}\|=\Big\|\sum_{n=N'+1}^{N}a_n\Big\|\le\sum_{n=N'+1}^{N}\|a_n\|=t_N-t_{N'}=|t_N-t_{N'}|.$$
Hence $(s_N)$ is Cauchy in $V$, and $V$ is complete, so $(s_N)$ converges. $\blacksquare$

## 3. Proof of the Main Theorem

Fix the enumeration $n\mapsto j_n$ of $J$ and, for $N\in\mathbb N$, set
$$F_N:=\{j_0,j_1,\dots,j_N\}\cap S .$$
Each $F_N$ is a finite subset of $S$, and $F_0\subseteq F_1\subseteq F_2\subseteq\cdots$.

### Step 1: partial sums are finite subset sums over $S$

Since $n\mapsto j_n$ is injective, it restricts to a bijection $\{0,1,\dots,N\}\to\{j_0,\dots,j_N\}$.
A finite sum in an abelian group is unchanged under re-indexing along a bijection (generalized
commutativity), so
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N}v_{j_n}=\sum_{i\in\{j_0,\dots,j_N\}}v_i,\qquad
  \sum_{n=0}^{N}\|v_{j_n}\|=\sum_{i\in\{j_0,\dots,j_N\}}\|v_i\| .$$
If $i\in\{j_0,\dots,j_N\}\setminus S$ then $v_i=0$ and $\|v_i\|=0$, so those terms may be dropped:
$$\boxed{\ \sum_{n=0}^{N}v_{j_n}=\sum_{i\in F_N}v_i,\qquad
  \sum_{n=0}^{N}\|v_{j_n}\|=\sum_{i\in F_N}\|v_i\|\ }\tag{3.1}$$

### Step 2: the supremum of the partial sums of norms is $M$

Write $t_N:=\sum_{n=0}^N\|v_{j_n}\|$. By (3.1) and the definition of $M$ we get $t_N\le M$ for all
$N$, since $F_N$ is a finite subset of $S$.

Conversely let $F\subseteq S$ be finite. If $F=\varnothing$ then $\sum_{i\in F}\|v_i\|=0\le t_0$.
Otherwise, since $F\subseteq S\subseteq J$ and $n\mapsto j_n$ is a bijection onto $J$, every $i\in F$
is $j_{n(i)}$ for a unique $n(i)\in\mathbb N$; put $N:=\max\{n(i):i\in F\}$, which exists because $F$
is finite and non-empty. Then $F\subseteq\{j_0,\dots,j_N\}$ and $F\subseteq S$, so $F\subseteq F_N$,
and since all terms $\|v_i\|$ are $\ge0$,
$$\sum_{i\in F}\|v_i\|\ \le\ \sum_{i\in F_N}\|v_i\|\ =\ t_N .$$
Taking the supremum over all finite $F\subseteq S$ and combining with $t_N\le M$:
$$\sup_{N\in\mathbb N}t_N=M. \tag{3.2}$$

### Step 3: proof of part 1

$(t_N)_{N\in\mathbb N}$ is non-decreasing, because $\|v_{j_{N+1}}\|\ge0$. A non-decreasing sequence of
reals converges iff it is bounded above, and then its limit is its supremum. By (3.2), $(t_N)$ is
bounded above iff $M<\infty$, and in that case $\lim_N t_N=M$. That is:
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty\|v_{j_n}\|\ \text{converges}\iff M<\infty,\ \text{ and then }
  \sum_{n=0}^\infty\|v_{j_n}\|=M. \tag{3.3}$$
The hypotheses on $K$ are identical to those on $J$ (countably infinite, $S\subseteq K$, enumerated by
a bijection), so the same argument verbatim gives
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty\|v_{k_n}\|\ \text{converges}\iff M<\infty,\ \text{ and then }
  \sum_{n=0}^\infty\|v_{k_n}\|=M. \tag{3.4}$$
Since $M$ does not depend on which of $J,K$ (or which enumeration) we used, part 1 follows: the two
series converge absolutely under exactly the same condition $M<\infty$, and then their sums of norms
are both $M$. $\square$

### Step 4: proof of part 2

Assume $M<\infty$. By (3.3), (3.4) and Lemma 2.1 both series converge in $V$; write
$$L:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{j_n}=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{n=0}^{N}v_{j_n},\qquad
  L':=\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{k_n}.$$

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $M<\infty$ is the supremum in its definition, there is a finite
$F\subseteq S$ with
$$\sum_{i\in F}\|v_i\|>M-\varepsilon. \tag{3.5}$$

*Claim:* $\|L-\sum_{i\in F}v_i\|\le\varepsilon$.

As in Step 2 there is $N_0$ with $F\subseteq\{j_0,\dots,j_{N_0}\}$, hence $F\subseteq F_{N_0}$ and so
$F\subseteq F_N$ for every $N\ge N_0$. For such $N$, using (3.1),
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N}v_{j_n}-\sum_{i\in F}v_i=\sum_{i\in F_N}v_i-\sum_{i\in F}v_i=\sum_{i\in F_N\setminus F}v_i,$$
whence by the triangle inequality
$$\Big\|\sum_{n=0}^{N}v_{j_n}-\sum_{i\in F}v_i\Big\|\le\sum_{i\in F_N\setminus F}\|v_i\|
 =\sum_{i\in F_N}\|v_i\|-\sum_{i\in F}\|v_i\|\le M-\sum_{i\in F}\|v_i\|<\varepsilon,$$
where we used $F\subseteq F_N$, then $F_N\subseteq S$ finite so $\sum_{i\in F_N}\|v_i\|\le M$, and
finally (3.5). Letting $N\to\infty$ and using continuity of $x\mapsto\|x-\sum_{i\in F}v_i\|$ (a
consequence of the reverse triangle inequality), the claim follows.

The set $F$ is a finite subset of $S\subseteq K$, so exactly the same argument applied to the
enumeration $n\mapsto k_n$ gives $\|L'-\sum_{i\in F}v_i\|\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$$\|L-L'\|\le\Big\|L-\sum_{i\in F}v_i\Big\|+\Big\|\sum_{i\in F}v_i-L'\Big\|\le2\varepsilon .$$
As $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary, $\|L-L'\|=0$, i.e. $L=L'$. $\blacksquare$

## 4. The corollary, in its corrected form

> **Corollary 4.1 (the intended statement).** Under the hypotheses of the Main Theorem, and for any
> $r$: the series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{j_n}$ converges absolutely to $r$ if and only if the series
> $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{k_n}$ converges absolutely to $r$ — under reading (A) ("absolutely convergent
> with vector sum $r$", $r\in V$) and equally under reading (B) ("absolutely convergent with
> $\sum_n\|v_{j_n}\|=r$", $r\in\mathbb R_{>0}$).

*Proof.* By symmetry in $J$ and $K$ it suffices to prove one direction. Suppose
$\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{j_n}$ converges absolutely to $r$.

Absolute convergence of $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{j_n}$ means $\sum_{n=0}^\infty\|v_{j_n}\|$ converges, so
$M<\infty$ by (3.3); by (3.4) $\sum_{n=0}^\infty\|v_{k_n}\|$ converges too, i.e.
$\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{k_n}$ converges absolutely.

Under (A): by Main Theorem part 2, $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{k_n}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{j_n}=r$.
Under (B): by Main Theorem part 1, $\sum_{n=0}^\infty\|v_{k_n}\|=M=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\|v_{j_n}\|=r$.
Either way $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{k_n}$ converges absolutely to $r$. $\blacksquare$

> **Corollary 4.2 (enumeration independence / unconditional convergence).** In particular, taking
> $J=K$, the value of $\sum_{n=0}^\infty v_{j_n}$ and of $\sum_{n=0}^\infty\|v_{j_n}\|$ do not depend
> on the chosen enumeration of $J$: an absolutely convergent series in a Banach space may be
> arbitrarily rearranged without changing its sum.

*Proof.* Two enumerations of $J$ are two admissible choices of enumeration in the Main Theorem with
$K=J$, so parts 1 and 2 apply. Concretely, for the rearrangement statement: let $\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n$
be an absolutely convergent series in $V$ and let $\sigma:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ be a bijection. Apply
the Main Theorem to $I=J=K=\mathbb N$, $v_i:=a_i$, with the enumerations $j_n:=n$ and $k_n:=\sigma(n)$
of $\mathbb N$; the hypothesis $S\subseteq J\cap K=\mathbb N$ is automatic, and $M<\infty$ by (3.3)
since $\sum_n\|a_n\|=\sum_n\|v_{j_n}\|$ converges. Hence $\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_{\sigma(n)}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n$
and $\sum_{n=0}^\infty\|a_{\sigma(n)}\|=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\|a_n\|$. $\square$

> **Corollary 4.3 (what survives of the literal reading).** Keep the hypotheses of the Main Theorem
> and take the series from $n=1$, as literally written. Then:
> 1. $\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_{j_n}$ converges absolutely $\iff M<\infty\iff\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_{k_n}$
>    converges absolutely. (So the *unquantified* statement "one converges absolutely iff the other
>    does" is true even literally.)
> 2. If $M<\infty$, then
>    $$\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_{j_n}=L-v_{j_0},\qquad \sum_{n=1}^\infty v_{k_n}=L-v_{k_0},$$
>    $$\sum_{n=1}^\infty\|v_{j_n}\|=M-\|v_{j_0}\|,\qquad \sum_{n=1}^\infty\|v_{k_n}\|=M-\|v_{k_0}\|,$$
>    where $L$ and $M$ are as in the Main Theorem.
> 3. Consequently, if $M<\infty$, the literal biconditional holds
>    * for every $r\in V$ under reading (A) $\iff v_{j_0}=v_{k_0}$;
>    * for every $r\in\mathbb R_{>0}$ under reading (B) $\iff \|v_{j_0}\|=\|v_{k_0}\|$.
>
>    In particular $v_{j_0}=v_{k_0}$ — which holds, for instance, whenever $j_0,k_0\notin S$, both
>    terms then being $0$ — is sufficient under either reading. If $M=\infty$ the literal
>    biconditional holds vacuously, both sides being false for every $r$.

*Proof.* (1) Deleting the single term $n=0$ changes neither the convergence of a series nor the
convergence of its series of norms; and by (3.3), (3.4), $\sum_{n=0}^\infty\|v_{j_n}\|$ and
$\sum_{n=0}^\infty\|v_{k_n}\|$ converge exactly when $M<\infty$.

(2) For $N\ge1$ we have $\sum_{n=1}^{N}v_{j_n}=\sum_{n=0}^{N}v_{j_n}-v_{j_0}$. When $M<\infty$ the
right-hand side converges to $L-v_{j_0}$ as $N\to\infty$ by the Main Theorem, so
$\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_{j_n}=L-v_{j_0}$. The other three identities are the same computation, using
part 2 of the Main Theorem for $K$ and part 1 for the two series of norms (whose full sums are both
$M$).

(3) Assume $M<\infty$; by (1) both series converge absolutely, so under either reading the truth of
"$\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_{j_n}$ converges absolutely to $r$" is just the equation "sum $=r$".

Reading (A): if $v_{j_0}=v_{k_0}$ then by (2) the two sums coincide, so each side of the
biconditional is the same statement and the biconditional holds for every $r\in V$. If
$v_{j_0}\ne v_{k_0}$ then $L-v_{j_0}\ne L-v_{k_0}$; taking $r:=L-v_{j_0}$ makes the left side true and
the right side false.

Reading (B): if $\|v_{j_0}\|=\|v_{k_0}\|$ then by (2) the two sums of norms coincide and the
biconditional holds for every $r$. If $\|v_{j_0}\|\ne\|v_{k_0}\|$, say $\|v_{j_0}\|<\|v_{k_0}\|$, put
$r:=M-\|v_{j_0}\|$. Then $r>M-\|v_{k_0}\|\ge0$, so $r\in\mathbb R_{>0}$ is admissible, the left side
holds and the right side fails. (Here $M-\|v_{k_0}\|\ge0$ because $M-\|v_{k_0}\|$ is the sum of the
convergent series of non-negative terms $\sum_{n\ge1}\|v_{k_n}\|$.)

Finally, if $M=\infty$ then by (1) neither series converges absolutely, so both sides of the
biconditional are false for every $r$ and it holds vacuously. $\blacksquare$

## 5. Summary

The corollary is true and is exactly the assertion that, for a family in a Banach space whose
non-zero members all lie in two countable sets $J$ and $K$, the absolute convergence and the value of
the resulting series are independent of which of $J,K$ and which enumeration is used; the common
value of the sums of norms is $M=\sup\{\sum_{i\in F}\|v_i\|: F\subseteq S\ \text{finite}\}$. The only
defect in the statement as posed is the index range $n\ge1$ against enumerations starting at $j_0$,
$k_0$, which makes the literal biconditional false (§1) and is repaired by summing from $n=0$.
